learningObjectives.title: Musical elements and structures (fugue, sonata, concerto)

questions.q: Which dates best describe the Baroque period in Western classical music?
questions.explain: The Baroque era ran from around 1600 to 1750, often dated as ending with the death of J.S. Bach in 1750.

questions.q: Which composer is a leading figure of the Baroque period?
questions.explain: J.S. Bach (1685-1750) is one of the most important Baroque composers, famed for his fugues and choral works.

questions.q: Which keyboard instrument is most characteristic of Baroque music?
questions.explain: The harpsichord, which plucks its strings, was the standard Baroque keyboard and typically played the continuo part.

questions.q: In a fugue, what is the name given to the main melodic idea stated at the opening?
questions.explain: A fugue opens with the subject, a short melody that is then imitated in turn by the other voices.

questions.q: What are the three main sections of sonata form, in order?
questions.explain: Sonata form comprises the exposition (presenting the themes), the development (varying them) and the recapitulation (restating them).

questions.q: In a Baroque concerto grosso, what is the small group of solo players called?
questions.explain: The concertino is the small group of soloists, contrasted with the larger ripieno (or tutti) ensemble.

questions.q: Who composed the Symphony No. 101 in D major, nicknamed 'The Clock'?
questions.explain: Joseph Haydn, a central Classical composer, wrote Symphony No. 101 'The Clock' as one of his London symphonies.

questions.q: Which dates best describe the Romantic period in Western classical music?
questions.explain: The Romantic era spanned roughly 1810 to 1910, following the Classical period.

questions.q: 'Terraced dynamics', where the volume shifts suddenly between levels rather than gradually, are typical of which period?
questions.explain: Baroque instruments like the harpsichord could not easily crescendo, so composers used sudden, block-like changes in dynamics.

questions.q: What is the function of the basso continuo in Baroque music?
options: To provide a continuous bass line and fill in harmonies
To play the solo melody throughout
To mark the beat with untuned percussion
To sing the words of a chorus
questions.explain: The continuo, usually a keyboard plus a bass instrument, supplies a running bass and improvises chords above it.

questions.q: In a fugue, at which interval does the 'answer' normally enter in relation to the subject?
questions.explain: The answer is the subject transposed to the dominant, typically a fifth above (or a fourth below) the original.

questions.q: In the exposition of a sonata-form movement in a major key, in which key is the second subject usually heard?
options: The relative minor of the dominant
questions.explain: In a major-key movement the second subject typically appears in the dominant, creating tonal contrast with the tonic first subject.

questions.q: An accompaniment that breaks a chord into a repeated pattern of low-high-middle-high notes is known as an Alberti bass. Which period is it associated with?
questions.explain: The Alberti bass was a common left-hand keyboard accompaniment in the Classical period, giving a light, clear texture.

questions.q: Ritornello form, in which a recurring orchestral theme alternates with contrasting passages, is most closely associated with which genre?
questions.explain: Baroque concertos often use ritornello form, where the tutti 'ritornello' returns between solo episodes.

questions.q: In a Classical concerto, what is a cadenza?
options: A virtuosic solo passage, often unaccompanied, showcasing the soloist
questions.explain: The cadenza is a showy, often improvised or unaccompanied passage that lets the soloist display technical brilliance.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Romantic music?
options: Programme music that tells a story or depicts a scene
questions.explain: Romantic composers frequently wrote programme music, using instrumental works to depict narratives, emotions or scenes.

questions.q: The second movement of Haydn's Symphony No. 101 features a steady, staccato accompaniment in the bassoons and pizzicato strings. What does this feature explain?
options: The 'ticking' that gives the symphony its nickname 'The Clock'
The use of a fugal exposition
The presence of a solo cadenza
The terraced dynamics of the Baroque
questions.explain: The regular, ticking staccato accompaniment in the Andante is the source of the symphony's nickname 'The Clock'.

questions.q: You hear a Baroque work in which a full orchestral theme keeps returning between passages played by a small group of soloists. Which structure is being used?
options: Ritornello form in a concerto grosso
questions.explain: The recurring tutti theme alternating with soloist passages is ritornello form, typical of the Baroque concerto grosso.

questions.q: In a sonata-form movement, you notice the first and second subjects both return, now firmly in the tonic key. Which section are you hearing?
questions.explain: In the recapitulation both subjects return in the tonic, resolving the tonal contrast set up in the exposition.

questions.q: In a Classical piano sonata you see the left hand playing continuous broken chords beneath a clear melody. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Continuous broken-chord patterns in the left hand supporting a melody are an Alberti bass, characteristic of Classical keyboard music.
